summary: Correct 240 L wheelie-bin silhouette (tapered body, overhanging lid, rear handle and wheels on the same side) but it reads as a smooth, dark, untextured CG block with a crude axle box.
critique: Proportions are broadly right (about 1.07 m high, tapering body, lid overhang). The rear handle is a nice bent tube, and the close-up shows a rounded rim lip. What breaks it: (1) The axle/wheel housing is a full-width rectangular box that reads as a solid plinth. Real bins have a moulded rear skirt with two recessed wheel arches and a visible steel axle; the wheels sit mostly OUTSIDE the body footprint. The wheels look about 160 mm and thin; real ones are 200 mm diameter, 50-60 mm wide solid rubber with a hub. (2) The lid is a flat slab. There is no hinge knuckle row across the back, no front grip lip or overhang tab, and no shallow ribbing on top. (3) The body faces are perfectly flat. Real bins have vertical stiffening ribs or recesses on the sides and front, a front lifting comb (a horizontal flange about 100 mm below the rim for the lorry lifter), and the front foot/bumper pads. (4) Material: uniform near-black, no roughness variation, no embossed capacity/standard text, no hot-stamped council crest or house-number sticker, no scuffs, grime streaks or dried drips. As a result it reads as plastic-coloured clay.
suggestions: Replace the full-width axle box with a moulded rear skirt: two wheel arches about 220 mm high, wheels 200 mm diameter x 55 mm, outside the body width, joined by a visible 20 mm steel axle. About 300 tris.
Add the front lifting comb, a horizontal lip about 40 mm deep running full width about 120 mm below the rim, plus two front foot pads. About 60 tris.
Lid: add a hinge knuckle row (5-6 short cylinders) at the back, a 30 mm front grip overhang and 2-3 shallow raised ribs on top.
Body: inset 3-4 shallow vertical recess panels per side (10 mm deep) so light breaks across the faces.

Material: a 512 px trim/decal sheet with an embossed '240L EN 840' block, a white council sticker and a painted house number. Raise roughness to about 0.6 with lighter dusty grime toward the base, edge scuffs on the rim and handle, and a darker greasy streak under the lid front. Lift the albedo to about 0.06-0.08 (charcoal), not near-black, or swap the variant colour to council green/grey/blue.
renderer_notes: The side faces in the profile view go almost pure black; part of that is the missing ambient bounce, not the asset.

summary: Believable striped corner post with a spring base and a nicely wind-shaped flag; the cloth is faceted and the attachment and finish are too clean.
critique: The best of this batch. The post height (about 1.5 m) and the red/white banding are right, and the black spring base is a good, correct detail. The flag has a convincing wind-blown fold. Problems: (1) Up close the cloth is visibly faceted, with jagged triangular edges along the free side and hard polygon creases. Real nylon flags have smooth rolling folds and a hemmed edge. (2) The flag has no attachment: no sleeve, ties or plastic clip at the top of the pole, so it looks glued to the pole. It also hangs from the very top with no top cap or finial ring. (3) Flag size looks under the 500 mm minimum: it reads as about 400 x 450 mm. (4) The pole stripes are perfect flat paint with hard edges. There is no scuffing at the base from mowers or boots, no grass stain, and the plastic shows no specular variation. (5) The spring looks right but the ground socket/base cup is missing: real ones sit in a ground sleeve with a visible rim.
suggestions: Smooth the flag: increase the cloth grid to about 12 x 12, apply one smoothing pass to the displacement, and add a 10 mm hem strip along the free edges (a darker albedo band in the texture). About 300 tris.
Add a flag sleeve/clip: a 60 mm tall cylinder slightly wider than the pole at the top and middle of the flag's pole edge, plus a domed top cap. About 80 tris.
Scale the flag to 500 x 500 mm minimum, per the Laws of the Game.
Add a 90 mm diameter ground sleeve rim flush with the turf at the base of the spring.
Material: fabric roughness about 0.8 with a subtle weave normal; pole roughness about 0.35 with base grime/grass stain up to 150 mm and slight colour fade on the red.
renderer_notes: The flag's pure white is close to clipping in the sun; that's partly exposure, but the albedo should also be capped at about 0.8.

summary: A clean white goal frame with a convincing hex net, but nothing makes it read as PORTABLE: no wheels, base frame or counterweights, and the beige pebble 'weights' look like rocks.
critique: The frame proportions (a wide, low mouth) and the hex net are good, and the net sag reads well in the close view. Problems: (1) A portable goal is defined by its freestanding rear: a ground frame (rectangular tube along the back and sides), rear wheels (2-4 small pneumatic or solid wheels on the back bar or on flip-down axles), and anti-tip counterweights (steel boxes or sandbags). This model has a bare triangular side frame and two small beige oval blobs at the post bases that read as stones, not sandbags. (2) The net has no visible back-top support: the net simply slopes from the crossbar to the ground. Portable goals normally have a rear top bar or net stanchions giving a box shape. (3) Frame tubes are uniform white with no joints: no corner brackets, bolts, net hooks/clips along the bar, or ground-bar welds. (4) Materials are pristine. There's no scuffing on the posts, no grass staining on the ground bar, and no wear at the bottom of the net. (5) The net shows a wavy horizontal band partway down the back panel that looks like a mesh artefact.
suggestions: Add the portable base: a 60 x 60 mm or 50 mm round rear ground frame forming a rectangle with the posts (depth about 1.5-2.0 m), and two or four 200 mm wheels on the rear corners (or on a lift-bar axle). About 600 tris.

Replace the beige blobs with proper counterweights: dark green or black PVC sandbags (saddle shape over the ground bar, about 600 x 300 x 120 mm) or steel weight boxes. Or remove them and let the wheels and ground bar carry the read.
Add a rear top bar or two net stanchions so the net forms a box/stepped profile, and anchor the net to it with clip loops every 300 mm.
Add corner brackets (box sleeves) at the crossbar/post and post/ground-bar joints, plus a row of small net-clip bumps along the crossbar's back. About 200 tris.
Material: frame roughness about 0.4 with grey-green grime at the base (bottom 200 mm), scuffs on the posts at ball height; net albedo slightly off-white about 0.7.
Investigate and remove the wavy band in the rear net panel.
renderer_notes: Shadow and lighting fine; the net aliasing is acceptable.

summary: A plain black cylinder with cream bands and a domed cap: recognisable as a bollard light but toy-like, with no lens, louvres or fixing detail; the close-up view shows no head detail at all.
critique: (1) Scale: it reads tall, around 0.9-1.0 m, and fat. Typical path bollards are 450-600 mm high (some to 900) and 100-110 mm diameter (some 200), and this one is around 150-180 mm. (2) The light head is the whole point and it is just two opaque cream bands separated by black rings. Real bollard heads have a frosted/opal polycarbonate diffuser (slightly translucent, emissive at night) under a louvred or slotted cap, or a 360-degree glare-shield louvre stack with gaps showing the lamp. (3) There is no base detail: no flange plate, no fixing bolts, no access door with a security screw, and no ground plinth. (4) Material: flat matte charcoal with no powder-coat orange-peel, no dirt splash at the base, and no specular. (5) The close-detail view looks down past a featureless grey shaft to a white disc, so it offers nothing to check; the head is likely being culled or clipped in that camera.
suggestions: Rescale to about 600 mm high x 110 mm diameter (or offer 600/900 variants).

Rebuild the head as 3-4 stacked louvre rings with real gaps (5-8 mm) through which an inner opal diffuser cylinder is visible. Give the diffuser an emissive channel and albedo about 0.85 with slight transmission. About 400 tris.
Add a cast base flange (about 150 mm diameter, 10 mm thick) with 3-4 bolt heads, and a small rectangular access door outline about 300 mm up.
Material: powder-coat charcoal (albedo about 0.05, roughness 0.45) with a fine orange-peel normal, mud/grass splash darkening on the bottom 80 mm, and a manufacturer label sticker near the base.
Fix the close-detail camera so it frames the head.
renderer_notes: The close-up framing problem is in the review camera setup, not necessarily the asset.

summary: Three bright red beveled slabs floating above the ground, with no supports and broken shading: placeholder level.
critique: (1) It has no structure at all: three planks hovering about 0.4 m in the air with no legs, frames, brackets or mounting rail. Even a stadium bench plank that mounts to a riser should ship with its brackets/pedestals. (2) The planks are very thick (around 100 mm) and almost touching, and look about 1.2 x 0.9 m: more like a mattress. Real plank benches use 3-5 slats about 95-145 mm wide x 35-45 mm thick with 10-15 mm gaps. (3) The bevel shading is badly broken: smooth-shaded normals across the bevel produce twisted diagonal gradients and a swirled dark band along each slat, plus a visible triangulation crease in the close-up. That reads as warped plastic. (4) The material is saturated pinkish-red with high gloss, with no wood grain or plastic moulding texture and no wear. If it's meant to be painted timber, the paint should show grain and edge chips; if recycled plastic, the colour should be muted with a matte, slightly mottled finish.
suggestions: Add supports: two cast/steel pedestal legs or a galvanised box-section frame (40 x 40 mm) at about 450 mm seat height, with bolt heads through each slat. Or, for a terrace version, two brackets that mount to a step. About 300-500 tris.
Resize the slats to about 1800 x 120 x 40 mm with 12 mm gaps (4-5 slats) and a 3-5 mm bevel.
Fix the normals: split normals at the bevel (or use a weighted-normal rule: face normals on the flat faces) so the faces shade flat and only the bevels catch the light.

Material: if painted timber, use a tileable 512 px wood-grain normal/albedo with paint chipping at the edges and ends (exposed grey timber). Use a less saturated red (sRGB about 150,30,30) with roughness about 0.55 and greying from dirt along the gaps.
Ground it: the seat must touch the ground via the legs; no floating.
renderer_notes: The odd diagonal gradients are the asset's normals, not lighting.

summary: The trapezoid 8-yard skip shape and yellow paint are right, but the rubble sits on a flat yellow LID: the skip has no open top or interior, and the steel is pristine.
critique: (1) The biggest error: the top is a closed flat yellow plate and the rubble is heaped on top of it. A skip is an open steel box; you should see the inside walls, a 50-80 mm thick top rim channel around the edge, and the rubble sitting inside at or below rim level. (2) The proportions are about right (a long, sloped-end trapezoid of roughly 3.4 m top length, 1.7 m wide and 1.2 m high), but the walls have no thickness and no rim. (3) The vertical ribs are thin raised strips; real skips have pressed or folded channel ribs and a heavy top rim section, plus a hinged drop door on one end with locking bars on some models. (4) The lifting lugs are small grey cylinders; real lugs are chunky forged trunnions about 80 mm in diameter with a retaining collar, and there are usually 4 (plus 2 tipping lugs at the base). (5) Material: flat clean yellow with no rust streaks, dents, chipped paint, stencilled hire-company name/phone number, chevron reflectors or a lamp bracket. Real skips are among the most battered objects on a street. (6) The rubble is mostly near-identical grey blocks over a strangely smooth mottled 'sheet' with pink spots, and lacks varied debris such as timber, plasterboard and bags.
suggestions: Make it open: build the walls with 5 mm thickness plus an inward-rolled 60 x 60 mm rim channel. Model the floor and inner walls, and place the rubble pile inside so its top is about 100-200 mm below or slightly over the rim. About 300 tris.

Rubble: 3-4 rubble meshes (brick chunks, a broken plasterboard sheet, timber offcuts, a black builder's bag, a twisted metal strip) scattered on a lumpy fill surface coloured dusty grey-brown. Keep it under 1.5k tris with instancing of chunks.
Ribs: replace the strips with trapezoidal pressed channels (about 60 mm deep), and add a horizontal channel near the base.
Lugs: four chunky trunnions (80 mm diameter, 100 mm proud, with a collar disk) on the sloped ends near the top, plus two lower tipping lugs.

Material/decals: a 1k texture with rust drip streaks from every rib and lug, a dent normal map, chipped paint showing dark steel on the rim, a stencilled 'SKIP HIRE 01234 567890' on the side, red/white reflective chevron panels on the ends, and darker grime on the bottom 300 mm. Albedo yellow about sRGB (200,160,30), roughness 0.65.
renderer_notes: The end face in the profile view renders very dark brown; part of that is the lack of ambient bounce in shadow.

summary: A plain square stick with an orange-painted top and a tiny nail: correct concept but greybox-level in shape, scale and material.
critique: (1) Scale: it reads as about 1 m tall and 80 mm square, more like a fence post. Typical timber survey pegs are 25-50 mm square and 300-600 mm long, driven in so that only 100-300 mm shows (taller ranging stakes exist, but they are thinner laths). (2) Shape: a perfect prism with razor-sharp edges and no top. Real pegs have sawn, slightly rough ends, a battered or flattened mushroomed top from hammering, splits, and usually a sharpened point (hidden in the ground, but the base should enter the ground with some disturbance). (3) The orange paint is a clean block with a hard line; real marking paint is sprayed, with overspray fading down the sides and drips, and the top often carries a nail with a washer or a coloured flagging tape tied around. (4) The wood has no grain, uses only flat colours, and one face goes nearly black. (5) No ground interaction: there is no little mound of disturbed soil or hammer marks around the base.
suggestions: Rescale to 50 x 50 mm with about 300 mm exposed (add a 450 mm variant), and an 'in ground' depth of about 150 mm below grade.
Bevel edges by 2-3 mm and add a slightly crushed/mushroomed top (a few vertices pushed outward and down). About 40 tris.
Add a 2 mm survey nail with a 15 mm washer on top, and an optional fluorescent flagging tape loop: a ribbon strip with two hanging tails about 150 mm. About 60 tris.

Material: a 256 px sawn-softwood albedo/normal (pale yellowish timber, about sRGB 170,140,100) with grain, plus a sprayed-paint gradient mask on the top 80 mm with overspray fade and mud on the bottom.
Add a small disturbed-soil decal or mound at the base.
renderer_notes: The near-black shaded face is partly from no ambient bounce, but the albedo is also too dark.

summary: Reads as a white bathroom-sink pedestal rather than an outdoor drinking fountain: smooth untextured clay, with no bubbler, drain or push-button detail worth the name.
critique: (1) Material/identity: matte white with no specular makes it look like ceramic or unshaded clay. Outdoor drinking fountains in UK parks and training grounds are powder-coated steel (dark green/black/grey) or brushed stainless, or cast iron/concrete. (2) Shape: the column is a plain flared cylinder and the bowl a flat dish with a shallow rim. Real units have a dished stainless bowl with a central drain grille, a raised bubbler nozzle with an anti-contamination guard (a hooded shroud), and a push-button or lever on the front face of the column, chunky and clearly marked. Here the 'spout' is a thin grey rod lying across the bowl and the button is a small cylinder on the side. (3) Proportions: the bowl rim at about 0.95-1.0 m looks right, but the column is too fat relative to the bowl, so it reads as a sink. (4) No base fixing plate, access panel, bottle-filler, accessibility lower bowl, or signage ('Drinking water'). (5) No wear: no limescale ring in the bowl, water staining, splash marks at the base, or chipped coating.
suggestions: Change the material to powder-coated steel (dark green sRGB about 30,60,45 or graphite, roughness 0.45) with a brushed-stainless bowl (metallic 1.0, roughness 0.3, anisotropic-looking streak texture).
Model the bowl properly: a 300 mm diameter dish about 60 mm deep with a raised lip, a central drain grille disk (slot pattern in the texture), and a 40 mm bubbler with a hooded guard. About 300 tris.
Slim the column to about 180-200 mm diameter (or square 200 x 200), add a 250 mm square base plate with 4 bolt heads, and a rectangular access panel with 2 security screws.
Move the push button to the front face: a 50 mm diameter stainless disc in a 70 mm boss. Optionally add a bottle-filler alcove on the side.
Wear/decals: a limescale ring and water stain in the bowl, wet darkening on the ground at the base, a 'Drinking Water' plate decal, and chipped coating on the edges.
renderer_notes: The flat white may be partly exposure, but the material still needs specular and colour.
